cues.text: The captain’s son
Paolo Maldini was born in Milan, Italy, in 1968.
His father, Cesare, had been a defender and the captain of AC Milan and of Italy.
At sixteen, Paolo played for Milan’s first team, and he was given the number three shirt his father had once worn.
In 1986, his father even called him up to Italy’s under-21 team.
Lift the name tag on the paper shirt.
Following a famous parent can bring a lot of pressure.
But Paolo’s path was his own.
He began as a winger, became a right-back at fourteen, and later made the left side his home.
You don’t have to be your parent. You only have to be yourself.
So close with Italy
With Italy, Paolo came very close to the biggest trophies.
At the 1990 World Cup, Italy lost the semi-final on penalties.
In 1994, they lost the World Cup final to Brazil on penalties.
In 1998, they went out on penalties again, to France.
Flip the scoreboard through the years.
At Euro 2000, Italy led the final 1–0 until the very last minute, and then France won in extra time.
Paolo never won a trophy with Italy.
Still, he played 126 games for his country, and he was captain for eight years.
You are more than one result. Be proud of how hard you tried.
Captain in the hard years
After coach Fabio Capello left in 1996, Milan had disappointing seasons.
For two seasons in a row, they did not qualify for European competitions.
In 1997, when Franco Baresi retired, Paolo was made Milan’s captain, in the middle of the struggles.
Tap three times to clear the storm clouds.
Paolo led the team through it, and in 1999 Milan won the Serie A title by one point.
Then came more hard seasons.
Being a leader does not mean everything goes well.
It means you keep showing up.
Hard seasons pass. Keep going, and keep helping the people around you.
The finals that got away
Paolo also knew the pain of losing big finals.
Milan lost the Champions League final 1–0 to Marseille in 1993, and 1–0 to Ajax in 1995.
The hardest night came in 2005, in the final against Liverpool.
Paolo scored in the very first minute, and Milan led 3–0 at half-time.
Turn the paper clock to the second half.
Liverpool fought back to draw, and then won on penalties.
Paolo later called it the worst moment of his career.
A loss like that can hurt for a long time.
It’s okay to feel sad after a loss. Talk about it with someone you trust.
Two years later
In 2007, Milan reached the Champions League final again, in Athens.
Their opponents were Liverpool, once more.
This time, Milan won 2–1.
At 38, Paolo became the oldest captain ever to lift the trophy.
Flip the calendar from 2005 to 2007.
In all, Paolo won that trophy with Milan five times: in 1989, 1990, 1994, 2003 and 2007.
The worst night of his career did not stop him.
It was not the end of his story.
A terrible night can be followed by a great one. Keep going.
Not everyone cheered
Paolo played his last home game at San Siro, Milan’s stadium, in May 2009.
The crowd gave him a standing ovation.
But a group of Milan’s own fans, called ultras, protested against him as he said goodbye.
Even after twenty-five seasons, not everyone cheered.
Raise the number three shirt.
Milan retired it, so no one else would wear it.
In 2016, Paolo’s father Cesare, who had worn that number before him, died at 84, and his mother Marisa died later that year.
Losing a parent is sad at any age.
Not everyone will cheer for you, and that’s okay. Hold on to the people who love you.
